extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, translators, and students of verse
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and judging poetry derived from Horace's Ars Poetica and translator's notes: emphasis on wisdom, craft, plausibility, revision, audience, and the moral/social function of verse. Suitable for poets seeking classical practical rules for literary composition and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisdom as the foundation of good writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Of writing well, be sure, the secret lies In wisdom: therefore study to be wise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought (wise, serious ideas) must come before words: study philosophy and serious thought (e.g., 'the page of Plato') because 'found, the words will come as soon as sought.' The implication: strong, intelligent ideas are primary; eloquence without wisdom is hollow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match sentiment to role/part
rubrics_metrics.description: The man who once has learned to comprehend ... That man, when need occurs, will soon invent For every part its proper sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand duties, social relations, and character aims so you can invent the appropriate tone and sentiment for each dramatic or poetic role. Know your characters' obligations and relationships to supply fitting emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe life and manners for 'living words'
rubrics_metrics.description: Look too to life and manners, as they lie Before you: these will living words supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground diction and incidents in real-life observation; everyday manners and behavior provide the concrete materials that make language vivid and believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content (thoughts and morals) over empty versification
rubrics_metrics.description: A play, devoid of beauty, strength, and art, So but the thoughts and morals suit each part, Will catch men's minds ... More than the clink of verses without thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work whose ideas and ethical fit are right will engage readers even if its versification is not ornate; avoid prettiness that lacks substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise; favour short maxims in lecturing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whene'er you lecture, be concise: the soul Takes in short maxims, and retains them whole: But pour in water when the vessel's filled, It simply dribbles over and is spilled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overlong didacticism and verbosity. Present maxims briefly; overcrowding an audience/readers with too much will cause loss of impact (antipattern: long-winded moralising).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain plausibility and internal truth in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep near to truth in a fictitious piece, Nor treat belief as matter of caprice. If on a child you make a vampire sup, It must not be alive when she's ripped up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect internal logic and reader credulity: improbable or inconsistent details (e.g., a vampire scene that violates earlier premises) break trust. Ensure events and facts cohere within the work's world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance instruction and pleasure (mix grave and gay)
rubrics_metrics.description: But he who, mixing grave and gay, can teach And yet give pleasure, gains a vote from each: His works enrich the vendor, cross the sea, And hand the author down to late posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to instruct without forfeiting enjoyment; blend seriousness and levity so different audiences benefit—didactic sole aim or mere amusement alone is less enduring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgive minor slips but not chronic faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Some faults may claim forgiveness: for the lyre Not always gives the note that we desire; ... A blot or two I readily condone, Such as may trickle from a careless pen, Or pass unwatched: for authors are but men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasional blemishes are tolerable in an otherwise excellent work; small lapses can be excused, but they should be rare and not systemic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid recurring errors or persistent incompetence
rubrics_metrics.description: the copyist who keeps stumbling still At the same word had best lay down his quill: The harp-player, who for ever wounds the ear With the same discord, makes the audience jeer: So the poor dolt who's often in the wrong ... Moves but fresh laughter at his own expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated, identical mistakes demonstrate entrenched incompetence and deserve sharp criticism; eliminate recurring faults through revision and training (antipattern: habitual sloppiness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider how a work is received at distance vs close inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Some poems, like some paintings, take the eye Best at a distance, some when looked at nigh. One loves the shade; one would be seen in light, ... One pleases straightway; one, when it has passed Ten times before the mind, will please at last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that different works reward different modes of reading: some please immediately, others grow on readers with repeated exposure; design pacing and detail accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mediocrity; middling poetry is shunned
rubrics_metrics.description: But gods, and men, and booksellers agree To place their ban on middling poetry. ... Just so with verse; you seek but to delight; If by an inch you fail, you fail outright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better to abstain than to produce mediocre verse; small shortcomings often doom a work's reception—aim for clear merit rather than lukewarm competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both nature and art are necessary; train your talent
rubrics_metrics.description: But here occurs a question some men start, If good verse comes from nature or from art. For me, I cannot see how native wit Can e'er dispense with art, or art with it. Set them to pull together, they're agreed, And each supplies what each is found to need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innate talent must be disciplined by craft; rigorous practice, study, and technical learning complement natural gifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline and practice precede public performance
rubrics_metrics.description: The youth who suns for prizes wisely trains, Bears cold and heat, is patient and abstains: The flute-player at a festival, before He plays in public, has to learn his lore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare and endure training before public display; do not rely on casual or untrained performance (antipattern: boastful unprepared 'bardlings').

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not depend on hired or flattering audiences; seek honest judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: As puffing auctioneers collect a throng, Rich poets bribe false friends to hear their song: ... If you write poems, look beyond the skin Of the smooth fox, and search the heart within. Read verses to Quintilius, he would say, 'I don't like this and that: improve it, pray:'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware flattering listeners and paid applause; prefer frank, critical readers who will point out faults rather than sycophants who overpraise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrust work to candid critics and revise thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrust it first to Maecius' critic ears, Your sire's, and mine, and keep it back nine years. ... A wise and faithful counsellor will blame Weak verses, note the rough, condemn the lame, Retrench luxuriance, make obscureness plain, Cross-question this, bid that be writ again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek rigorous external critique, accept substantive corrections, prune excess, clarify obscurities, and be prepared to rewrite. Consider delaying publication (even years) until work is sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold back publication; what's sent abroad cannot be revoked
rubrics_metrics.description: What's kept at home you cancel by a stroke: What's sent abroad you never can revoke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution before making work public; unpublished material can be erased, but publication is permanent—revise thoroughly before release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's public and moral function
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse taught life's duties, showed the future clear, And won a monarch's favour through his ear: Verse gave relief from labour, and supplied Light mirth for holiday and festal tide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember verse can instruct, regulate behaviour, correct social vices, and serve communal/ritual functions; consider the ethical and civic roles of your poetry when shaping content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose words carefully; select and reject with discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: In words again be cautious and select, And duly pick out this, and that reject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice careful diction—prune weak or superfluous words, prefer clarity and aptness; revision should include active culling of unnecessary phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious altering well-known tales or characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Than alter facts and characters, and tell In a strange form the tale men know so well.... It is hard to treat hackneyed subjects with originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not change established stories or central character traits lightly; tampering with familiar material risks outraging readers unless handled with clear rules and strong justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master technical forms and metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Yet so that none should ask it to resign The sixth, fourth, second places in the line. ... I introduced [translational aids] for the benefit of persons ... who may attempt to write Iambic trimeters with no guide but this passage
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn metre, line-positions, and formal constraints; technical mastery eases composition and prevents metrical mistakes (antipattern: attempting complex forms with no knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with 'new phrases'; prefer sanctioned usage
rubrics_metrics.description: New phrases, in the world of books unknown, So use but father them, he makes his own. I understand 'quae genitor produxerit usus' ... as words already sanctioned by usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coinage and novelty should be handled carefully; prefer words that have established usage in literature unless you can successfully 'father' innovations into common use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid writing driven solely by profit
rubrics_metrics.description: O, when this cankering rust, this greed of gain, Has touched the soul and wrought into its grain, What hope that poets will produce such lines As cedar-oil embalms and cypress shrines?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money-motivation corrupts poetic quality; poets who write for profit or bribe audiences tend to produce inferior work. Aim for artistic integrity rather than commercial gain.
